group.title: Health and the body
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: A pain in your belly.
examples: I ate too much cake and now I have a {stomachache}.
wrong: My stomachache is in my left ear.

words.meaning: A pain in a tooth or in your teeth.
examples: She went to the dentist because of her {toothache}.
wrong: I have a toothache in my foot.

words.meaning: A pain inside your ear.
examples: The loud music gave him an {earache}.
wrong: My earache hurts the bottom of my foot.

words.meaning: A pain in your back.
examples: Carrying heavy boxes gave me a {backache}.
wrong: I have a backache in my eye.

words.meaning: An illness like a bad cold, with a high temperature and pain all over.
examples: He stayed home for a week with the {flu}.
wrong: The flu made her feel full of energy and very well.

words.meaning: A common, mild illness that gives you a runny nose and a cough.
examples: I have a {cold}, so I keep sneezing.
wrong: I have a cold, so I feel perfectly healthy today.

words.meaning: When liquid keeps coming out of your nose because you are ill.
examples: I need tissues because I have a {runny nose}.
wrong: My runny nose is completely dry.

words.meaning: To become ill with a mild illness that makes you sneeze.
examples: Wear a coat or you’ll {catch a cold}.
wrong: I caught a cold, so I felt better than ever.

words.meaning: To feel that you might bring food up from your stomach.
examples: I {feel sick} when I read in the car.
wrong: I feel sick, so I’d love a big plate of food right now.

words.meaning: To become healthy again after being ill.
examples: Drink lots of water and you’ll {get better} soon.
wrong: She got better, so she had to stay in the hospital longer.

words.meaning: A sweet liquid medicine you drink to stop coughing.
examples: Take a spoon of {cough syrup} before bed.
wrong: I put cough syrup on my cut knee.

words.meaning: The part in the middle of your arm where it bends.
examples: He hit his {elbow} on the table.
wrong: She bent her leg at the elbow.

words.meaning: The part of your leg just above your foot, where it bends.
examples: She fell and hurt her {ankle}.
wrong: He wears his watch on his ankle near his hand.

words.meaning: The part of your arm that joins it to your hand.
examples: She wears a watch on her {wrist}.
wrong: My wrist is between my knee and my foot.

words.meaning: The part of your face below your mouth.
examples: He has a small beard on his {chin}.
wrong: She put her hat on top of her chin.

words.meaning: The part of your face above your eyes.
examples: Mom touched my {forehead} to see if I was hot.
wrong: He wears glasses on his forehead to see better.

words.meaning: One of the two soft sides of your face below your eyes.
examples: The baby has round pink {cheeks}.
wrong: She has a cheek on the bottom of each foot.

words.meaning: The line of hair above each eye.
examples: He raised one {eyebrow} in surprise.
wrong: My eyebrows grow on my chin.

words.meaning: One of the two soft edges of your mouth.
examples: Cold wind makes my {lips} dry.
wrong: He wears his lips on his fingers.

words.meaning: The soft part inside your mouth that you use to taste and speak.
examples: The soup was so hot it burned my {tongue}.
wrong: I tasted the soup with my elbow, not my tongue.

words.meaning: The front part of your body between your neck and your stomach.
examples: He felt a pain in his {chest} when he coughed.
wrong: My chest is the part of my body under my feet.

words.meaning: The short, thick finger at the side of your hand.
examples: The baby sucks her {thumb}.
wrong: I put my thumb in my shoe next to my toes.

words.meaning: One of the five small parts at the end of your foot.
examples: I hit my {toe} on the door.
wrong: She wears a ring on her toe of her hand.

words.meaning: One of the two sides of your body below your waist.
examples: She stood with her hands on her {hips}.
wrong: His hips are on his head, just above his ears.

words.meaning: A visit to a doctor or dentist to see that you are healthy.
examples: I go to the dentist for a {check-up} twice a year.
wrong: A check-up is a party with cake and music.

words.meaning: To bring food back up from your stomach through your mouth.
examples: The boat moved so much that he {threw up}.
wrong: She threw up her lunch, so it stayed in her stomach.

words.meaning: Ill; not feeling healthy.
examples: She felt {unwell}, so she went home early.
wrong: He was unwell, so he ran a marathon full of energy.

words.meaning: A room where people sit until the doctor can see them.
examples: We sat in the {waiting room} for twenty minutes.
wrong: The doctor operates on patients in the waiting room.

words.meaning: To put your body flat on a bed or the floor to rest.
examples: If you feel dizzy, {lie down} for a while.
wrong: She lay down by standing up very straight.

words.meaning: To not get up because you are ill or tired.
examples: The doctor told me to {stay in bed} for two days.
wrong: I stayed in bed all day, walking around the city.

words.meaning: To push air out through your nose into a tissue to clear it.
examples: Here’s a tissue, so you can {blow your nose}.
wrong: I blew my nose by drinking a glass of water.

words.meaning: Causing pain; hurting a lot.
examples: A broken leg is very {painful}.
wrong: The injection was painful, so I didn’t feel anything.

words.meaning: A picture of the inside of your body, made by a special machine.
examples: The {x-ray} showed that his arm was broken.
wrong: She took an x-ray of the beach with her phone.

words.meaning: Making you want to scratch your skin.
examples: The mosquito bite is red and {itchy}.
wrong: My skin is itchy, so I don’t want to touch it at all.

words.meaning: Connected with health and treating people who are ill.
examples: You need a {medical} test before you start the job.
wrong: She studied medical science to learn how to build cars.

words.meaning: A chair with wheels for people who cannot walk.
examples: After the accident he used a {wheelchair} for a month.
wrong: He sat in his wheelchair because he loved to run.

words.meaning: To stay healthy and strong by doing exercise.
examples: I swim twice a week to {keep fit}.
wrong: She keeps fit by sitting on the sofa all day.

words.meaning: A piece of soft paper you use to clean your nose.
examples: Can I have a {tissue}? I need to sneeze.
wrong: I wrote a long letter on a tissue and posted it.

words.meaning: To hurt a joint by turning it the wrong way.
examples: He {twisted} his ankle playing soccer.
wrong: She twisted her ankle, so it felt stronger than before.

words.meaning: To fall to the ground from standing.
examples: The little boy {fell over} and cut his knee.
wrong: He fell over and stayed standing the whole time.
